content.title: Correct and non-trivial, but not at the same time
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.review:
To paraphrase a well-known review, the paper is in part correct and in part non-trivial. Unfortunately, these parts do not overlap.

The chief correct statement is that training deep networks for classification or regression yields embeddings in which the intended classification or regression task can be performed adequately via nearest neighbors in the learned embedding space. That is, after training, we can strip out the final linear classifier or regressor and replace it by nearest neighbor classification or regression in the same embedding space in which the linear classifier or regressor operates. In other words, the embedding learned via backprop is so good that linear classification or regression in this space can be replaced by nearest-neighbor interpolation. This is well-known and is not surprising. This observation predates the recent resurgence of interest in neural networks, but is well documented in recent work as well. See, for example, Razavian et al., "CNN Features off-the-shelf: an Astounding Baseline for Recognition" (1.5K citations). The authors try to claim some novelty in that they apply this well-known observation to pixel-level prediction networks, but the reviewer fails to see what in this application was non-trivial or surprising.

The paper then suggests that this effectiveness of the Euclidean metric in the final embedding space learned by backprop is in a way the underlying operating principle of the learned model, that in some deep sense the learned network “really is” a nonparametric classifier or regressor in a more pertinent sense than it is a parametric model. That the model is functionally and ontologically a nearest neighbor machine rather than a parametric model. Depending on how one interprets this proposition, it is either trivial or unsubstantiated.

Let’s begin with the trivial: Of course a deep network can be viewed as a nearest neighbor machine. The network was trained to minimize a regression or classification loss on the training samples. It must minimize the loss over the samples. The training samples are the only data it has. Of course the output of the model over the training data and nearby points in the embedding space will be identical or similar to the training labels and can thus be regarded as “memorization”. Since the training data is the only thing that is given, everything the training procedure does can be interpreted as “memorization”. But that is a trivial perspective that does not contain a novel insight.

Now to the unsubstantiated implication. As discussed earlier, training a compositional nonlinear embedding with a linear classification or regression loss in the final layer also yields an embedding in which the Euclidean distance works well. From this the authors appear to conclude that the network is in essence a nearest neighbor machine more so than it is a classifier or a regressor. If we try to go beyond the sense in which this statement is trivial, we reach a false dichotomy: why can’t a model trained for classification or regression also construct an intermediate representation in which the Euclidean metric is effective? This may just be a useful thing to do if one needs to apply a linear classifier or regressor in the embedding space. Arranging the data so that the Euclidean distance works well is a perfectly sensible thing for backprop to do. Why does that make the model more of a nearest neighbor machine than a compositional nonlinear classifier or regressor? Why can’t a parametric model trained to construct layers of nonlinear embeddings and perform linear classification or regression on top also yield a final embedding in which the Euclidean distance works? This can be regarded as a “spandrel”, to borrow a term from evolutionary biology: a property that emerges (as a byproduct) while optimizing for a different objective. The fact that the Euclidean distance works in the final embedding space doesn’t make the model a nearest neighbor machine in any sense beyond the obvious one discussed earlier. Yes, training a deep network for classification or regression yields an embedding in which the Euclidean distance works well, but the network is still a parametric model trained for classification or regression.


The issues covered so far are a sufficient basis for my rating. I will now cover some other issues:

- The term “generative” is misused in the paper. For example, the pix2pix model is taken as an example of a generative model. It's not. pix2pix is a discriminative model. It is trained in a supervised fashion, on input-output pairs, to perform discriminative regression. The models studied in the paper are discriminative models, not discriminative and generative models.

- The term “compositional” is misused in the paper, at least in relation to the general use of this term in the literature. “Compositionality” in the literature generally refers to hierarchical composition with representations of increasing scope. This is the sense in which language is said to be compositional. It is also the sense in which “compositionality” was used in the work of Zeiler and Fergus, which is cited in this context in the submission. But the paper uses “compositional” in a different and rather trivial sense. The analogue in the language domain would be to say that language is compositional because it is composed of letters. This is strictly speaking true, but it is not the compositionality that people generally care to discuss in the representation learning field. This trivial application robs the term “compositional” of its richer and more important meaning.

- The paper contains phrases such as “novel interpretation of neural networks as learning hierarchies of embeddings” (page 6). This interpretation is not novel. It is one of the central guiding intuitions in deep learning and has been with the field from its earliest days.


Other comments:

- SegNet is referred to as “a recent state-of-the-art network for image segmentation. SegNet is a fine model, but it’s not state-of-the-art, at least in terms of standard benchmarks and leaderboards. SegNet can be a convenient model to use in experiments because it’s fast. This is a perfectly good motivation, but in this case it should be stated upfront, without hiding behind the misapplied “state-of-the-art” term.

- For the quantitative evaluation (Table 1), pix2pix is used as a semantic segmentation baseline for the Cityscapes dataset. This is very strange. Why not use a semantic segmentation model to perform semantic segmentation? The authors have already set up SegNet and are using it for semantic segmentation. Why not use SegNet as the semantic segmentation baseline on Cityscapes?

- For quantitative evaluation of semantic segmentation (Table 1), the authors report overall pixel accuracy (fraction of correctly classified pixels). This is a terrible and misleading measure that is generally avoided in the literature. The issue is that the measure is dominated by large classes that are easy to classify, such as sky, road, and building. This means that simplistic models perform well and that differences between poor models and good ones can be quantitatively insignificant. For these reasons, experienced researchers don’t trust this measure. Mean per-class accuracy and mean IoU are more reliable.

content.title: usage of term "compositional"
content.comment:
Q: The term “compositional” is misused in the paper, at least in relation to the general use of this term in the literature. “Compositionality” in the literature generally refers to hierarchical composition with representations of increasing scope. This is the sense in which language is said to be compositional. It is also the sense in which “compositionality” was used in the work of Zeiler and Fergus, which is cited in this context in the submission. But the paper uses “compositional” in a different and rather trivial sense. The analogue in the language domain would be to say that language is compositional because it is composed of letters. This is strictly speaking true, but it is not the compositionality that people generally care to discuss in the representation learning field. This trivial application robs the term “compositional” of its richer and more important meaning.


We agree that we use composition in somewhat of a “flat”, rather than hierarchical sense. However, our use of the term has been proposed before - e.g., “Similarity by Composition”, Boiman & Michal Irani NIPS 2006. We clarify this in the last paragraph on page 2. From the NLP perspective, one can define regular grammars for modeling language (Chomsky, 1956), which can be seen as “flat” N-gram markov models for generating words. Our results in Table 1 (revised version) also show that such composition considerably improves performance over naive nearest neighbor matching.

That said, we quite agree that CNNs get much of their power from hierarchical processing. Figure 3 suggests such “flat” compositional matching is happening at each intermediate layer of a network - that is, each layer takes an input an embedding and spits out a new embedding (typically for a larger image patch corresponding to a larger receptive field). We believe that this successive chaining of embeddings allows the CNN to gradually learn a semantically-rich pixelwise embedding at the last layer.

content.title: novel aspects
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback, and highlight the surprising aspects of our work: 

Q: In other words, the embedding learned via backprop is so good that linear classification or regression in this space can be replaced by nearest-neighbor interpolation. This is well-known and is not surprising.

While using the learned embedding with a nearest-neighbors (NN) seems straightforward, there are non-trivial aspects of this embedding that this work discusses. Unlike classical CNNs for image classification that encode global properties of an image, the embeddings for pixel-level tasks contain local (e.g., window styles or  facade decorations) and global (e.g., color and style of a facade) information. Moreover, this work shows that by using a NN classifier or regressor with a cosine distance on the patch-embeddings allows us to not only understand the network biases but also correct it (Fig 9 (Fig 8 in original version)). Finally, our results show that nearest neighbor interpolation can be used to replicate the behaviour of internal layers of a deep network (Fig 3). We are not aware of prior work that show this, but would be happy to add any citations.

As we replied to R1, it is hard to argue that our results are surprising  because this is somewhat subjective. Note however that R2 does find our results “striking”, and the non-review post find it “fascinating, believable”. We argue that these observations are *useful* for interpreting the network, understanding its biases, and finally, manipulating the behaviour of a network. “Explaining by example” is a well-known approach to model interpretability that dates back at least to [Caruna et al “Case-based explanation of non-case-based learning methods” 1999]. For example, consider a radiologist who would like an explanation of why an x-ray of a tumor was automatically classified as ‘malignant’. One such explanation might be that it looks similar to particular training exemplars. We demonstrate that exemplars can be used to intuitively explain CNN predictions, which have been historically characterized as “black-boxes” (or “alchemy”, to quote a recent and heated public discussion). Moreover, Fig 9 (Fig 8 in original version) shows that we can manipulate the behaviour of a network (without re-training) by manipulating the set of exemplars being matched to. For example, this simple observation can be used to manipulate the biases of a face recognition network that may be biased toward certain races or genders. 

From a technical point of view, explaining-by-examples is fundamentally limited by the size of the training set. We demonstrate that one can explain exponentially more through composition  - rather than N exemplars, we can generate (NK)^K outputs (assuming an image of K pixels - see Page 2, Para 2).  Finally, we show that such explanations can also be used to interpret the internal layers of a network.  Importantly, internal layers are not trained as features for linear classifiers, but still exhibit the same behavior.

content.title: review: lacking novelty and actual insight
content.review:
This paper purports to analyze whether convolutional neural networks (CNNs) behave as compositional nearest neighbors, in the context of pixelwise prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation or Pix2Pix [Isola et al, 2016].

But, nearest neighbors in what feature space?

If this paper showed that CNNs emulated nearest neighbors according to L2 distance between patches in pixel space, that would be quite a result.  Alternatively, if it showed CNNs emulated nearest neighbors in some other human-engineered feature space, or even any feature space not obviously related to neural networks, it would also be quite informative and impressive.

However, no such connections are made.  Rather, the feature space in which CNNs emulate nearest neighbors is the feature space defined by the embedding produced by the penultimate layer of the CNN.  This offers no novel insight.  Rather, it hides the real action of the CNN that goes into producing that embedding.  The production of the embedding may have absolutely nothing to do with nearest neighbors at all!

Moreover, it was already well established that CNNs produce useful generic feature representations that can be ported to a variety of visual tasks [Donahue et al, DeCAF: A Deep Convolutional Activation Feature for Generic Visual Recognition, 2013].

Looking at the penultimate layer representations, this paper experiments with replacing systems that, as trained, feed them into a single additional softmax classification or regression layer.  The replacement is to feed these features into a nearest neighbor classification layer.  It is not surprising that, given the same descriptive features as input, switching to nearest neighbors produces a similar result as the original linear classifiers.  This seems likely to be true in many settings, regardless of whether or not one is using a CNN.

Indeed, if patches x and y have feature representations phi(x) and phi(y), and for some classifier F, we approximate F(phi(x)) by F(phi(y)) where phi(y) is close to phi(x), how is it surprising that this approximation is good?

The fact, as the paper points out, that internal CNN layers could also be approximated this way, does not prove that the CNN is performing one big nearest neighbor operation.  The approximation seems to hold locally for the trivial reason that it would hold for almost any reasonable function F().

Finally, the paper claims (page 6), that its results suggest "one novel interpretation of neural networks as learning hierarchies of feature embeddings".  I believe virtually everyone in the computer vision community was already aware of this "novel" interpretation.  Since [Zeiler and Fergus, 2014], there has significant research in understanding how object and part representations emerge in intermediate layers of CNNs.

Note: Devlin et al, 2015 is duplicated in the references list.

content.title: Other concerns
content.comment:
Q: The paper claims (page 6), that its results suggest "one novel interpretation of neural networks as learning hierarchies of feature embeddings".  I believe virtually everyone in the computer vision community was already aware of this "novel" interpretation.  Since [Zeiler and Fergus, 2014], there has significant research in understanding how object and part representations emerge in intermediate layers of CNNs.


As both R1 and R3 strongly object to this line, we have removed it. But let us try to clarify. We demonstrate that intermediate layers can be used -- literally -- as  embeddings of image patches. We demonstrate this in Fig 3, and moreover use intermediate bottleneck embeddings to speed up our nearest-neighbor search (details in appendix). While this is well-known for the last feature layer (Devlin 2015, as we cite), we are not aware of prior work that demonstrates this for intermediate layers. Given the convolutional nature of intermediate layers, embeddings can be defined over local convolutional neighborhoods, allowing for composition. We are happy to be corrected and add any citations for previous work here! 

As an aside, we think embeddings are rather different from object-part representations. Embeddings follow a “distributed code” perspective (Learning Distributed Representation of Concepts, G. Hinton 1986) , while traditional parts and objects advocate a “sparse code” perspective (Learning Deep Architectures for AI, Bengio 2009). We believe that this distributed codes are one reason why CNNs outperform classic hierarchical models of parts/objects (e.g., Deformable Part Models, Felzenwalb et al 2010). Crucially, embeddings do not require individual activations to be semantically interpretable. Indeed, “Object Detectors Emerge in Deep Scene CNNs” (ICLR 14) points out that nearly half the neurons in a net are not interpretable when examined individually. From a mathematical perspective, nearest neighbors in an embedding will not change if one applies a well-behaved linear transformation (e.g., rotation) to the embedding space. This is consistent with past work (“Intriguing properties of neural networks”, ICLR14) that suggests that that  linear combinations of activations are equally as informative as the original activations. Finally, if high-level activations represent objects, how can ~4K activations (e.g., the dimensionality of FC7) represent 30K+ objects (Beiderman 1987)? One answer is that the activations do not represent individual objects, but rather the dimensions of an embedding space in which objects are points (matchable with nearest-neighbors). 


Q: “Moreover, it was already well established that CNNs produce useful generic feature representations that can be ported to a variety of visual tasks ”

This is quite true, but pointing out that a feature representation is generic is somewhat different than pointing out that a learning architecture seems to work by memorizing patches from its training set.

content.comment: Our goal is to provide an intuitive interpretation of CNNs . We agree that it would be interesting to explore nearest-neighbor matching of pixel features, but this is a novel algorithm rather than an analysis of CNNs. For the later, we explicitly analyze representations learned by CNNs. Our goal is not to “hide the real action”, but rather quite the contrary: we wish to emphasize the fact that CNNs intuitively work by learning remarkably good embeddings for matching and memorizing patches. The embeddings for pixel-level tasks are particularly rich in that they contain local (e.g., window styles or  facade decorations) and global (e.g., color and style of a facade) information.

content.title: rebuttal unconvincing
content.comment:
Having read the rebuttal and other reviews, I stand by my original rating of reject.

Nothing in the numerous comments by the authors addresses what seems to be the fundamental flaw, described in my original review, that reduces the results in this paper to a triviality:

"The feature space in which CNNs emulate nearest neighbors is the feature space defined by the embedding produced by the penultimate layer of the CNN."

Now, as argued in the rebuttal, this may be useful for visualization - but I do not believe that is substantially novel compared to established techniques of, for example, visualizing inputs that maximally activate particular output units.

Moreover, the paper is not written in a way consistent with visualization as a primary objective.  It clearly claims much more; the abstract claims to "understand and interpret the internal operations".  Here, the paper falls far short.

display_title: Interesting direction but limited analysis and potentially flawed method

content.title: Interesting direction but limited analysis and potentially flawed method
content.review:
This paper suggests that, on image synthesis and analysis tasks, convnets learn a function that is well approximated by a compositional nearest neighbor operation. In particular, running nearest-neighbor on the features of the last layer of a network, and copying over targets y from the matching pixels x in the training set, creates output images that look remarkably like those produced by the unmodified network. 

I think this is a neat paper with a lot of potential, but that potential is not yet fully tapped, and Eqn 7 seems to be contain critical flaw. 

First, Equation 7. Is the CNN referred to here the same CNN as the one being analyzed? My understanding of this equation is that a dictionary {x, f(x)} is constructed. Then we are given some new x_i, we look it up in the dictionary and find, let’s suppose, an exact match {x_i, f(x_i)}. At that point, we output the image f(x_i) as our “compositional nearest neighbor” result, and compare it to the actual output of f on x_i, which of course will exactly match since that is just f(x_i) again! Isn’t this tautological. It is simply fitting a nearest-neighbor approximation to f. With a big enough dictionary, it should come as no surprise that the approximation looks like the function it was fit to. As far as I understand, using Equation 7 completely invalidates the paper. However, Figure 4 suggests that something interesting may still be going on even without Equation 7, so I will give the rest of the review assuming that the gist of the paper will remain intact even with the method in Equation 7 removed.

It is intuitively compelling that CNNs are memorizing patches of the training set, but I would like to see more analysis of why this might be expected, of how the results in this paper can be explained in terms of network architecture, learning dynamics, etc. For example, what properties of a net would give rise to this behavior? I suppose if the feature activations are one-hot they and the columns of the weight matrix W are training exemplars, then the feature activations could act like lookups into the training set. It would be interesting to look at if something like this is happening. For example, characterize the sparsity of the features and the structure of W.

I think the most striking part of the paper are the figures, especially the maps in Figure 6 and the red lights at the bottom of the facade in Figure 6 row 2. The similarity between the CNN and nearest-neighbor make it quite clear that something eery is going on (assuming this is not just a trivial result due to Equation 7). Unfortunately, there is no quantitative analysis to dig deeper. The only quantification is Table 1, which seems tangential to the main point of the paper.

Unfortunately, while this paper might be onto something important, it is not acceptable in the present state due to the issue with Equation 7, and, even assuming that is not fatal, the lack of deep analysis makes this paper not ready for publication. But I think it’s a really interesting direction so hopefully will be further pursued!

Minor comments
1. What is the distance function “Dist”?
2. Repeated citation for Devlin et al. in the references section.

display_title: Concerns with Equation-7, and Deeper Analysis

content.title: Concerns with Equation-7, and Deeper Analysis
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and their encouragement to pursue this work. We address the concerns about Equation-7 in the revised version, and added more analysis to make it compelling.  In the following text, we address these concerns individually: 

Q: Equation 7 seems to contain a critical flaw.

In direct response to R2’s concerns, we have uploaded a new draft with new experiments where we use original labels {x_n, y_n}, instead of the self-supervised labels {x_n, CNN(x_n)}. Qualitative results in Appendix A and quantitative results in Table 1 (new draft) shows that original labels produce visually similar results with similar performance. We hope that this addresses the main concerns of R2 - self supervised labels smooth the results a bit (and so make for more pleasing visuals), but did not change any of the implications about memorization and compositionality. 

Q: It is intuitively compelling that CNNs are memorizing patches of the training set, but I would like to see more analysis of why this might be expected, of how the results in this paper can be explained in terms of network architecture, learning dynamics, etc. For example, what properties of a net would give rise to this behavior?

It would be interesting to understand the dynamics of learning and network architecture (“how” networks learn). However, the thesis of this work is to understand “what” the networks capture given standard architectures and learning mechanics. Towards that end, we introduce some theoretical motivation (Sec. 3.1) which suggests that the learned representation of most networks will capture sufficient statistics that memorize aspects of the data relevant for the task. The diversity of the networks in our experiments (SegNet, U-Net, etc.) suggests this may generally be true.

Q: I suppose if the feature activations are one-hot they and the columns of the weight matrix W are training exemplars, then the feature activations could act like lookups into the training set. It would be interesting to look at if something like this is happening. For example, characterize the sparsity of the features and the structure of W.”

In general, we find that feature activations are not one-hot. Our analysis suggests that exemplars correspond to points in the embeddings space, rather than one particular ”one-hot”  dimension of an embedding. In some sense, this corresponds to a “distributed representation” rather than a “sparse representation”.

Q: “Table-1 in paper and deeper analysis”: 

The purpose of Table-1 is to highlight that the performance on the final task does not suffer due to nearest neighbors and that one can expect an output that looks similar to what an end-to-end neural network would give. In the new version of the paper, we have added Figure 11 which highlights pixel correspondences in the generated output, input reconstruction in Figure 10, a theoretical discussion of why pixel-level representations are sufficient statistics for image generation (see Sec. 3.1), and additional qualitative results and analysis (see Appendix). We would be happy to add any more experiments the reviewer might have in mind!

Q: “What is the distance function “Dist”?
We use cosine distance. We added a new paragraph in Sec. 3 detailing implementation details.

display_title: A study to try and replicate your work

content.title: A study to try and replicate your work
content.comment:
As part of a multi-school project organized by Joelle Pineau, we (Max Rosen and Parker King-Fournier) have tried to reproduce the paper titled Do Convolutional Neural Networks act as Convolutional Nearest Neighbors? which was submitted by Chunhui Liu, Aayush Bansal, Victor Fragoso and Deva Ramanan to the 2018 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). The authors showed considerable evidence that convolutional neural nets for pixel-level tasks learn a fast compositional nearest neighbor synthesis/prediction function. The results were fascinating, believable and shed some light on the way convolutional neural nets may learn. 
While we were able to produce some results, we were unable to produce results consistent with the original paper and therefore cannot reach the same conclusion as the original authors. In attempting to replicate the study we came across some roadblocks that could not be avoided and identified some improvements which could be made to increase reproducibility.  
	One aspect affecting reproducibility that was seemingly unavoidable was the computational cost of the algorithm described in the paper. In order to be able to train our models in a reasonable amount of time, we were only able to train a predictor on one of the four datasets used. This is not inherently bad, but does make reproducing the results difficult for those without access to powerful computational tools. It would add a great deal to the original paper, and inform the reader of the scale of what is happening, to include information like training time, hardware used, etc. To give a sense of scale, we trained our Compositional Nearest Neighbor (CompNN)  model on the smallest dataset (The CMP Facades Database) for 8 hours on a 2016 MacBook Pro with 16GB of memory.
	It is noted in the paper that the model was pruned when the 1x1 layer of the neural net architecture was reached in order to speed up computation time for the decoding phase. The exact pruning mechanism was not described, so a pruning mechanism that considers the  k closest training examples was adopted, where k was arbitrarily chosen. This allowed for a considerable decrease in computation time.
 	During implementation, some assumptions were made where information was lacking. The CompNN function uses a distance function that was not specified: it was assumed to be the Euclidean distance. The architecture of the CompNN was also assumed. According to the authors, the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) Pix2Pix was used to created the architecture for the CompNN. Isola et al. reference two different architectures in their paper about Pix2Pix, however, there is no mention in the paper we reviewed as to which architecture was chosen to implement the CompNN algorithm. We chose to implement our recreation of the CompNN using the U-net architecture.

content.title: Revised Version
content.comment:
We have added following quantitative and qualitative analysis to further strengthen our work and make it more compelling: 

Quantitative Evaluation: We extended our quantitative evaluation in original version. In the revised version, we compare compositional nearest neighbors to the baseline CNN and different global nearest neighbor approaches, obtained by matching feature maps from different layers (R1’s concern). We now report both mean pixel accuracy and intersection-over-union, where predicted segmentation labels are compared to ground-truth labels (R3’s concern). We can observe in Table-1 that compositional matching approaches the accuracy of the baseline CNN, and dramatically outperforms global matching (sometimes by a factor of 2X). Finally, we address the concern of R2 regarding equation-7 and use of self-supervised labels. From Table-1, we observe that self-supervised labels (SS) overall perform similarly to the original labels (O) for compositional matching.

Qualitative Evaluation: We have added following  qualitative analysis in the revised version: 

1. Input Reconstruction: We added Figure 6 and Figure 10 to show that the learned embeddings of a CNN also enables the reconstruction of the input images in a compositional fashion

2. Correspondence: We added Figure 11 to show a correspondence map that explicitly illustrates how an output image is synthesized by cutting-and-pasting patches from training images.

3. Comparison between global nearest neighbors and compositional nearest neighbors: Throughout the new version, we have added the contrast between global nearest neighbors and compositional nearest neighbors. More specifically, Figure-1, 3, 6, 10, 12. 

4. More analysis about behaviour of different layers: We added Figure 4 where we show the outputs of matching using different layers for embedding. 

We have added discussion on “explanation-by-correspondence” in Section.1 (Introduction), and provided theoretical justification of sufficient statistics for pixel-level tasks in Section 3.1.

Finally, we have added more implementation details in Section-5 (Experiments) and an appendix containing more analysis and computational complexity.

content.title: after reading rebuttal and other reviews, still recommend rejection
content.comment:
After reading the discussion and paper revisions, I still think this paper is not ready for publication. I agree with the other reviewers that it is not clear if the results provide non-trivial insights. I still think there may be something here to push on (more on that below), but it is not coming across in the current paper.

I appreciate the addition of comparisons omitting Equation 7. However, I think Equation 7 should be removed entirely due to the issues I mentioned above. In fact, I now realize these issues also apply to the experiments on internal feature activations, and I think that section needs to be removed as well.

The reasoning is as follows (the same issue was pointed out by R1 as well). Suppose you have a function f(g(x)), where g(x) a net up to layer k and f the mapping to layer k+1. Then we try to explain this mapping by finding a training exemplar x_n such that g(x_n) is very close to g(x). Then it should be no surprise that f(g(x_n)) will be close to f(g(x)), assuming mild conditions on the smoothness of f. This is just fitting an NN approximation to the mapping learned by the network, which will always work with sufficiently large training data and sufficient smoothness of f. Since there is no analysis of the amount of data needed or the implied smoothness characteristics, this result provides no insight. Equation 7 is simply the case where k is the penultimate layer.

Despite these flaws, I think there may be something nontrivial in the finding that compositional nearest neighbor well approximates the mapping learned by the last layer of a CNN. However, the current paper does not do enough to convince the reader that this is a nontrivial result, nor to delve into any surprising implications. At first glance, the result does not look surprising since it is just replacing a small part of the network with a different model derived from the same training data. One would naturally expect that different regression models fit on the same data will tend to give similar results. What might be surprising or insightful is if it could be shown that there is better agreement between CNNs and compositional nearest neighbors than between CNNs and some other model. I expect there is a large class of models that would match CNN outputs similarly well. For example, linear regression.

In short, I do not think the observations about how CNNs are related to compositional nearest neighbors are sufficiently surprising, compelling, or precise to merit publication. However, what might remain interesting is how the method in this paper could be used to provide human digestible explanations of why a network is making the decisions it is making. Figure 11 is pretty interesting in this direction. It might be interesting to expand this analysis into a whole paper on network understanding and visualization (e.g., following the mold of papers like Koh & Liang ICML 2017).
